title: Image analysis-based quantification of fungal sporulation by automatic conidia counting and gray value correlation
author: Muskat, Kerkhoff, et al.
materials: Working with living fungal cells bears some error sources that can negatively affect the sporulation quantification by the developed method. In the present work, the conidia density on the Petri dish lid was insufficiently low to be detected by the developed method within the first 48 hours of sporulation from capsules. As far as the detectable conidia number threshold is not reached, the automatized counting can be applied but not the quantification by the gray value. Moreover, there is an upper limit of the conidia number quantifiable by the developed method based on a maximum gray value threshold. Furthermore, at high conidia densities, conidia are tending to stick together. The problem of segmenting sticking conidia was solved by the application of the watershed algorithm (see (Semi-)Automatic counting of conidia in the methodology). Another error source, also existing for other fungi, is the germination of conidia under suitable conditions. As shown in Fig. 7, after application of the watershed algorithm, the germ-tubes (Fig. 7A) are separated and counted as single particles (Fig. 7B).Fig. 7The germ-tubes of the conidia are separated by the watershed algorithm and counted as single particles.Fig 7

steps.title: Prepare collection surface
steps.instruction: Select a clear, clean, dry surface (Petri‑dish lid, glass slide, or similar). Clean it gently with an alcoholic solvent and a lint‑free paper tissue, avoiding scratches. Prepare blanks in the same way. If the surface is wet after conidia collection, dry it before imaging.

steps.title: Collect discharged conidia
steps.instruction: Expose the prepared surface to the fungus (or other organism) under conditions that allow conidia or other discharged units to settle onto the surface. Ensure the units are identifiable by bright‑field microscopy.

steps.title: Acquire bright‑field images
steps.instruction: Using a bright‑field microscope, capture images of the collected area. Typical image sizes are 500 × 500 µm² crops for detailed analysis or 2.5 × 2.5 mm² fields for density determination. Save images as 8‑bit files (gray values 0–255).

steps.title: Run automatic counting workflow
steps.instruction: Open each image in the image‑analysis software and execute the fully automatic workflow: segmentation, counting, and export of conidia numbers. This workflow processes an image in less than a minute.

steps.title: Run semi‑automatic counting workflow
steps.instruction: Open the image in the same software, set the required parameters manually (≈1 min per image), run segmentation, then inspect clusters. Apply the watershed algorithm to separate stuck conidia before final counting.

substeps.instruction: Inspect clusters and apply watershed to split them.
Count conidia and record the result.

steps.title: Extract gray‑value of each area
steps.instruction: For each analyzed field, record the mean 8‑bit gray value (range 0–255) of the corresponding sporulation zone.

steps.title: Calculate conidia density from gray value
steps.instruction: Convert the gray value (g) to theoretical conidia density (C, in cm⁻²) using Equation 2: C = 1250 ± 250 · g ± 8000. This provides a range in which the true density is expected to lie.

steps.title: Pseudo‑color image for visualization
steps.instruction: Apply a 6‑shade look‑up‑table to the 8‑bit gray‑value image to create a pseudo‑colored map of conidia densities. Example density values: outer zone ≈5 × 10⁴ cm⁻², intermediate zones ≈1.9 × 10⁵ cm⁻², and high‑density spots ≈1 × 10⁵ cm⁻².
